title: Vector data, indexes, and semantic search
summary: Store embeddings in the VECTOR type, measure similarity with VECTOR_DISTANCE, choose ANN vs ENN and DiskANN indexes — and compare vector support across databases.

items: Store embeddings in the VECTOR data type and query similarity with VECTOR_DISTANCE.
Choose the right distance metric (cosine, euclidean, dot).
Decide between ENN (exact) and ANN (approximate/DiskANN) search.
Compare vector capabilities with PostgreSQL (pgvector), MySQL, and Oracle.

blocks.body: Semantic search finds results by meaning, not keywords. SQL Server 2025 stores embeddings in the native `VECTOR` type and ranks by `VECTOR_DISTANCE`. At scale you add an approximate index (DiskANN). This lesson is the heart of Domain 3.

terms.definition: SQL Server 2025 data type storing a fixed-dimension embedding.
Function returning the distance between two vectors for a chosen metric.
Exact nearest neighbor — scans all vectors; perfectly accurate, slower.
Approximate nearest neighbor — uses an index (e.g., DiskANN) for speed at slight accuracy cost.
A disk-based ANN index used for large-scale vector search.

blocks.heading: The VECTOR type and distance
blocks.body: `VECTOR(n)` stores an n-dimensional embedding (documented cap 1,998 dims; float16 in preview halves storage). **`VECTOR_DISTANCE(metric, a, b)`** computes similarity for `'cosine'`, `'euclidean'`, or `'dot'`. Cosine is the usual choice for text embeddings. Order ascending by distance to get nearest matches.

blocks.heading: ENN vs ANN, and DiskANN
blocks.body: **ENN** (exact) scans every vector — perfect recall, fine for small sets. **ANN** (approximate) uses a **DiskANN** vector index for large corpora, trading a little recall for large speedups. On SQL Server 2025, DiskANN indexing is in **preview** and requires `PREVIEW_FEATURES = ON`. **`VECTOR_SEARCH`**, **`VECTOR_NORMALIZE`**, and **`VECTORPROPERTY`** are the related functions (several are in preview).

blocks.caption: Semantic search: embed the query, compare against stored vectors by distance, return top-k nearest neighbors.
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    query["User query text"] --> qembed["Embed query"]
    qembed --> dist["VECTOR_DISTANCE vs stored VECTORs"]

blocks.heading: Store and search vectors
blocks.body:
```sql
CREATE TABLE dbo.Doc (
    DocId int PRIMARY KEY,
    Body nvarchar(max),
    Embedding vector(1536)
);

-- Generate + store an embedding
UPDATE dbo.Doc
SET Embedding = AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(Body USE MODEL MyEmbedder);

-- Exact (ENN) top-5 semantic matches
DECLARE @q vector(1536) =
    AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(N'How do I reset my password?' USE MODEL MyEmbedder);

SELECT TOP (5) DocId, Body,
       VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', Embedding, @q) AS dist
FROM dbo.Doc
ORDER BY dist;
```

blocks.heading: Approximate search with a DiskANN index (preview)
blocks.body:
```sql
-- Requires PREVIEW_FEATURES = ON on SQL Server 2025
CREATE VECTOR INDEX vec_doc ON dbo.Doc(Embedding)
  WITH (METRIC = 'cosine', TYPE = 'diskann');

SELECT d.DocId, s.distance
FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(
       TABLE = dbo.Doc AS d,
       COLUMN = Embedding,
       SIMILAR_TO = @q,
       METRIC = 'cosine',
       TOP_N = 5) AS s
ORDER BY s.distance;
```

blocks.heading: PostgreSQL: pgvector
MySQL: VECTOR type + DISTANCE()
Oracle: AI Vector Search

comparison.title: Vector and AI capabilities
comparison.description: All four now offer vector types and ANN indexing; SQL Server and Oracle are closest in syntax, PostgreSQL uses pgvector operators, MySQL is the least mature for open-source ANN.

code.sqlserver: SELECT TOP 5 DocId FROM dbo.Doc ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', Embedding, @q);
code.postgresql: SELECT doc_id FROM doc ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5;
code.mysql: SELECT doc_id FROM doc ORDER BY DISTANCE(embedding, VEC_FROM_TEXT(?), 'COSINE') LIMIT 5;
code.oracle: SELECT doc_id FROM doc ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE(embedding, :q, COSINE) FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;

migration.equivalent: The store-embedding / order-by-distance pattern is identical everywhere.
migration.different: Index types (DiskANN vs HNSW/IVFFlat) and function vs operator syntax differ; MySQL open-source ANN is the weakest.
migration.directMigration: Yes for the query pattern; index DDL and distance syntax must be rewritten.
migration.syntaxChanges: Swap VECTOR_DISTANCE for pgvector operators or MySQL DISTANCE(); change index creation syntax.
migration.limitations: SQL Server DiskANN and several vector functions are in preview; MySQL open-source lacks mature ANN indexing.
migration.whenToUse: Choose the engine already holding your relational data so you avoid moving it — the core DP-800 value proposition.

blocks.heading: Semantic help-desk search over existing SQL data
blocks.body: Support articles already live in SQL Server. Add a `VECTOR` column, generate embeddings with `AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS`, and serve semantic search with `VECTOR_DISTANCE` — no data movement to a separate vector store. Add a DiskANN index once the corpus grows. This 'AI where your data lives' pattern is exactly what DP-800 validates.

items.mistake: Comparing vectors of different dimensions or models.
items.fix: All vectors must share the same dimension and be produced by the same embedding model.

items.mistake: Using ANN and expecting exact results.
items.fix: ANN trades recall for speed; use ENN when exactness matters or the set is small.
Smaller distance = more similar; order ascending for nearest neighbors.

blocks.body: Normalize vectors (VECTOR_NORMALIZE) when a metric requires it. DiskANN speeds large-scale search but is preview — validate recall. Apply RLS/permissions so semantic search can't surface rows a user shouldn't see.

tips: Cosine is the default metric for text embeddings; order ascending by distance.
VECTOR type, DiskANN, VECTOR_SEARCH have preview status on SQL Server 2025 — the exam may flag GA vs preview.
The whole point: run AI where the data already is, without moving it.

blocks.body: Store embeddings in VECTOR, rank by VECTOR_DISTANCE (cosine, ascending), and add a DiskANN index for ANN at scale. PostgreSQL (pgvector), Oracle (23ai), and MySQL 9 offer parallels; Oracle is closest in syntax. The DP-800 theme is doing AI in-database without moving data.
